title: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba”. Scope: naked protoplasm, amoeboid cells and pseudopodia

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The passive-versus-active alternatives imply distinct energy dependence and perturbation responses. Existing movies can test selected systems, though direct force measurements and mechanistic separation are incomplete.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track pseudopod-tip relaxation after local perturbation and compare curvature dynamics with capillary relaxation predictions; independently inhibit actomyosin contractility and alter membrane or cortical tension. Persistence of predicted rounding without active contraction supports the claim, while ATP-dependent contractile rounding refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern cortical tension often arises from active contractility.

Passive and active mechanisms may act together.

Direct tension measurements are uncommon.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Inhibition experiments can separate passive interfacial rounding from active contraction, and public image screens cover some of those perturbations. The decisive tension numbers are scattered, and the vocabulary of contractility has shifted since 1917, which makes the mapping only partly straightforward. For naked cells and blebs the test is informative; it is not yet a survey of protoplasm in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure rounding of protoplasmic drops and pseudopod tips when actomyosin contractility is inhibited and when interfacial tension is altered. Rounding that persists without contractility and follows interfacial tension would support the claim; rounding that requires active contractility would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern cortical tension is itself often generated by actomyosin, so 'vital contractility' needs a stipulated inhibitor.

Tension values are in papers more often than in the image archives.

Pseudopod tips and bulk cytoplasmic drops may not obey the same balance.
